utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. We apologise for the late start due to technical problems. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Douglas Stringer appearing on behalf of the Prosecution with Alexis Demirdjian, Antonio Garza, and our Case Manager Thomas Laugel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. For Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic, lead counsel; Christopher Gosnell, co-counsel; and Ms. Liane Aronchick, Case Manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: BORIVOJE SAVIC [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Savic. You were sworn in --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You were sworn in yesterday, and I remind you that you are still under oath. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Savic, I will play some video footage for you. This is something that you saw yesterday, because it was played to you by the OTP. I won't be playing the whole thing, just a section, the reason being there is a translation or interpretation error that occurred which we believe is quite relevant. This is at page 14, line 14. I will ask you to please try and listen very closely to a particular sentence that Mr. Goran Hadzic uttered, and please try and tell us, if you can, what exactly it was that he said. This is OTP Exhibit P53. We'll be looking at this section that starts at 4 minutes, 20 seconds into the clip, and it's a mere 10 seconds. It's up until 4:30 into the video-clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that the words were not translated or interpreted, the words spoken by Goran Hadzic. Witness, this section that you just heard, what did Goran Hadzic just say? Did he not say that the Croatian people should publicly give up on the Ustasha or did he say that they should publicly give up on the Ustasha policies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said they should publicly give up on the Ustasha.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is quite correct, because the record yesterday, the LiveNote, reflected Goran Hadzic as saying that the Croatian people should give up on their Ustasha policies, which gives the section a wholly different meaning, because as we ascertained yesterday, the Ustasha were merely a small group of political extremists. And what Goran Hadzic wanted in practical terms was for the Croatian people to give up on them, to renounce them. Thank you. Yesterday, we broke after we talked about the Obrovac meeting and what happened at Plitvice, if you remember. Something that we found slightly strange is the fact that you said that this was no arrest, but, okay, you are fully entitled to see it any which way you like. Nevertheless, at page 91, you say that you were prepared for the Plitvice harassment, that you were mentally prepared for something that was only to occur at a later stage. Can you please explain what exactly you meant by saying that? What sort of mental preparation did you undertake?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's not really anything special by way of preparation. You are prepared or ready at a given point in time to adapt to a certain situation depending on the circumstances, of course, as they say. A debate, is this a meeting, depending on the situation, as I said. So it's all a matter of instinct and intuition.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. You also say at page 50 of yesterday's transcript that in April 1991, you went to the Military Medical Academy. You went there because of what you had suffered at Plitvice. I want to know what exactly you got treatment for. Which specialists did you see? Did you undergo any particular specialist medical examinations at all while there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I arrived there late one evening. A man named Dr. Nikolic was there, and another man with a Macedonian surname. I told them I was there because there was no other hospital for me to go to. The incident had occurred a month before, perhaps, and I'm sure that they were aware of this. It was a regular exam, ear, throat, nose, that sort of thing. They checked my head. I think there were some fractures or fissures that were found, something like that. And then they just left me there lying in a bed. I can't really specify what examinations were performed, but it all had to do with the head and the ear, throat, and nose sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I assume you don't know which specialists looked at you during your time there at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You also say that between the 2nd of May, 1991, and sometime in November or December 1991, you spent some time in Serbia in a variety of different locations which you specified. You also explained what it was that you were doing there. What I want to know is were you actually gainfully employed? Were you contracted by anyone to be there and to work there? Is there any record of your time there, because you described all the jobs that you did when you were there, organising humanitarian aid, refugees, the territorial staff and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not remunerated for those jobs in any shape or form nor indeed did I sign any contracts. I covered my own expenses in all these cases, fuel, travel, accommodation, clothing. I covered all of that out of pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain? You had no salary. You weren't receiving any pay at all over those six or seven months. How on earth were you able to cover all your expenses? You would often spend nights at hotels. You would need to travel to get from point A to point B. Where did you get the money for all that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was my money, money that I had. Normally it would have been a perfectly usual thing at the time given the circumstances for people to loot and then sort of compensate themselves with these gains, the goods gained looting, but that's not something that I chose to do. I thought that I was perfectly able to pay my own way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would like to go back to a particular section of your statement, which is about what happened at Pakrac. That's between paragraph 49 and paragraph 61. I would like you to go through this with me. I'll be asking you a number of questions, because our information of some of these events contradicts yours. Our information suggests that what happened in Pakrac was the result of clashes between the reserve police who were there and the permanent police force based in Pakrac. So it wasn't a spontaneous outburst of any kind -- or, rather, it was a spontaneous outburst and not the result of something organised. You give an entirely different account of these events in your statement, so I would like to hear it from you. You state that the people from the SDS from Western Slavonia for all practical intents organised that attack, do you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Every time I state something it's open to debate and I'm perfectly happy to defend something that I said. I can do that by using documents, and I can try to argue my points. My information on Pakrac is a result of my activities at the time, the activities that I pursued in Western Slavonia specifically, Podravska Slatina, Lipik, Daruvar, Pakrac, that general area. We would have meetings there every two or three days. Western Slavonia was of particular interest, because this was where you first got to know about some people who simply showed up. New things started happening. There was this one time that a friend got in touch to tell me that Veljko Dzakula had left for Belgrade in order to arrange an action for Pakrac. All of the information in my possession was generated by well-meaning people who simply didn't have the courage to get involved, but they believed that if they passed some information on to me, perhaps I would be able to do something about it. So they meant well, in other words. They thought that I'd be able to prevent or stop something untoward from happening. So I went to Belgrade myself, straight to Metropol Hotel. I rang Veljko Dzakula's wife who lived in Belgrade. I told him where I was at the hotel, and whenever Dzakula arrived, I should like to meet him there, I said. He turned up at one point and said it's all been arranged. I said, What's been arranged? And he said, The action in Pakrac will start any time now. People are ready to fight. All they need is weapons. And this was the first I'd ever heard of anything like that, because we'd been adamant about the need to pacify everyone, to pacify the people there, to try and keep them calm. Just one little detail: Back in February 1991, they opened the building site for the elementary school in Soplje, near Podravska Slatina. President Mesic was there for the opening ceremony, Veljko Dzakula, Ilija Sasic and I were also to meet there in order to speak to President Mesic. I couldn't make it that day because of other commitments, but the next day we did meet. So I said, What happened? Veljko said, Mesic said there's every chance for our problem to be resolved. What chance and how exactly? And he said, Slobodan Milosevic after the elections for the first time agreed to talk about us, to discuss us. And what did you say? Would we agree for Slobodan Milosevic to be the one tackling our problem, tackling our issue? And then Mesic said, And what do you expect? Do you expect you'll be able to deal with this yourselves? And then I asked them, Did you get Mesic's message? And they said, Well, we understood exactly what he said. And I said, Do you understand that they're suggesting we need political guardians? We'll end up being a bargaining chip in this whole process. Don't stir up trouble with the people, because the people will be the ones paying the price, and there will be hell to pay. So this was the first I heard from Dzakula about this action in Pakrac. He said the army would be taking the area between the Hungarian border and the main road. So that part of Slavonia could split off, he said. What they talked about by referring it to -- by referring to it as a buffer zone. So the police would vote in favour of joining the police stations in Knin municipality and then the rest would follow in Dalmatia. And then he also said, We'll drive the police out like the Home Guard soldiers back in World War I wearing nothing but their nappies. We talked until 4.00 in the morning, and I tried to dissuade him. I tried to talk him out of it, and I said, Listen, you do this at your own risk. I told him in no uncertain terms that he would be receiving no support at all from us as a political party, and I said, You do as you see fit. Several days later, there was this action at Pakrac which was obviously co-ordinated and closely followed up, the result being what it was. The people there were given weapons. There was nothing those people could really do with their weapons. There were some infiltrators there, but there was no real fighting, nor was there supposed to be any real fighting there, but there was to be an act of provocation which would then trigger a police reaction. I said to Veljko, When people take up arms, they can no longer stay in the house. We organised meetings that were banned. We controlled that, but there was nothing provocative about them. That was not the intention. We were in charge of keeping order ourselves. I mean, there were some police officers there, too, but no one at all was allowed to attack those police officers, and we were pretty good at organising that kind of thing. So it's the uniform that keeps a policeman safe, and it also keeps the entire regime safe. If you attack a uniform, you attack the state. And we all know what happened. It was a planned operation. Everything was planned, and then people started moving out of the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll move on to a different subject now. You say in your statement, paragraph 91 specifically, that you advised members of the Serbian Democratic Party, Soskocanin in particular, to forward any and all requests directly to the government and not to people like Jovic, Seselj, Draskovic, et cetera. You remember that portion of your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Nevertheless, when reading your statement, I noticed that you make several references to your contacts with Nenezic, Kokot, Pekic, Kaloper. To the best of my knowledge, these were all retired generals, and I think most of them were members of the Communist League for Yugoslavia. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Some, some were. Kaloper was the party secretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Really, why were you in touch with these people while, on the other hand, you were telling everybody else to steer clear of the political parties and to only ever go directly to the state institutions, to the government, particularly bearing in mind what you said yesterday, that you were no Communist in terms of your political convictions. You had left the League of Communists long before. So why on earth were you now in touch with these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's not that I was in touch with these people. These were people who got in touch with me. It was the other way around, and then it doesn't really tally in terms of the time line. The contacts with Soskocanin were later, and these people, most of them left for Belgrade. I was the first to be invited, and I refused to go. And then since I was quite active, everybody who was on their way to Belgrade would confer with me. They'd ask questions and seek advice. It wasn't just Vukasin. I kept telling everyone the same thing. If you decide to go to Belgrade, the only possibly relevant thing is any promises that you can obtain from the government, not from the politicians. Some people favour Seselj, some people favour Vuk, and some people like somebody else, a different political party, particularly given the fact that all of these political parties were suddenly establishing volunteer brigades, Partisan brigades. Even Paroski set up a unit at the time. So it was just about sending people to the right address, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that time-wise things didn't tally, and I wanted to ask you this since we were unable to establish: Can you tell us when you were in contact with Nenezic? When did such contacts begin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I was in Belgrade in July. It was that period of time when Kaloper was there as well. I was invited to meet them from Slatina and the generals really tried to have their finger in every pie.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What about Pekic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was an incidental encounter on the premises in Cvijiceva Street where the Association of Croatian Serbs had their office. There was also an office there where Pekic received people. I was there because some of them had promised me a TV camera which had to be sent in the field. I happened to be there by chance at the door in the secretary's office. I had some time on my hands, and I was waiting for the people to go away, and I heard someone call out my name, Savic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You've already explained that in detail.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that's it, then. There's no need for me to explain any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm trying to establish this: You only saw Pekic once?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on -- upon his insistence. I did not seek contact with him. He did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we next have a look at a Prosecution exhibit? It is number 81 on the Prosecutor's list. Can you see it on the screen? We have the translation, but you will see the original text shortly as well in our language. That's the right page. I'm interested in the handwritten text in our language. I am not disputing the translation. I'd rather know something else from you. These were two separate sheets of paper, as far as I understood your statement, paragraphs 176 through 178. So there were two separate sheets. The upper portion of the text was written by Brana Crncevic, as you stated, whereas the lower portion was create by General Radojica Nenezic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we have it on our screens.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see -- I see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So the upper portion in our version was written by Brana Crncevic, as you say, and the lower portion was written by General Nenezic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He didn't write that. This paper was provided to him. He didn't write that, someone else did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I understand your statement as you saying that you had two separate sheets of paper provided by Crncevic and Nenezic respectively, and that on one of the sheets, you actually photocopied both those sheets on one piece of paper; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We can agree, I believe, that the lower portion of the text was written on a piece of paper which had horizontal lines.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it looks like it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what I can see, if you try to zoom in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was a plain notebook-style sheet of paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Whereas the upper portion was written on a clean sheet of paper without any lines.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You see in the lower portion there is something which I believe, and I stand to be corrected, that it was covered. It was crossed out. Can you see -- or basically there is -- there are lines missing, and then after a while we can see the lines continuing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I have the original still. So a photocopy was made. I can't recall why some text was covered. There was probably something underneath, but it's nothing secret. What was important was the list. I'll try to be brief. When I came to see General Nenezic, he showed me the paper. And he said, Just look at how they procure weapons. Apparently it was sent to him by Ilija Kojic or they believed him to be their warehouseman. That's what he was critical about. It had to do with the smuggling of weapons. So there were some alternative routes to procure weapons, and somebody simply tried their hand at obtaining weapons in that manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's not what I was interested in. Let's go back to what I asked you before. You say that some text on the lower sheet of paper was covered as it was not important.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So you covered that piece of text before photocopying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember. There's nothing there, nothing that would -- well, I have the original, and I can forward it if necessary. There was nothing to be hidden. I really can't say why I did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I saw in your statement that you handed this photocopy over to an OTP investigator.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you show him the original?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not. When I was preparing it, I photocopied it in that way. There's nothing special about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's look at that covered portion. We see three letters on the right-hand side followed by the number 30 in the original text. You see it there. It is my impression that the last three letters in the Cyrillic script are VIC with the diacritic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Is the first letter V?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That may well be. Perhaps like in the end letters of the last name Zivanovic, but then the number may be indicative of a house address. The street called Sanja Zivanovic is where Nenezic's house was. I don't know whether he lived at number 30, but that could be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But it could also be "Savic," do you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I might as well agree, but there's no need to, because there's no need -- well, even if it is "Savic," it's still not a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, I think, considering that there are weapons mentioned on this document, if there is a first and last name, I wouldn't say it's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you agree, I'm ready to bring the original to your office in Belgrade where you can scan it. There's no problem whatsoever regarding this piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Savic, I'll tell you this: What I dispute in your statement and what my position is, is that as of early May 1991 until the end of the war in 1995, you never met Goran Hadzic. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You said 1991?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As of May 1991. Say around the 6th, 7th, or 8th of May, 1991, until the end of 1995, you never met with Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said yesterday we met in Lovas, and I stand by that. We also saw each other -- now, what year was that? In any case, when there was an attempted removal of the president of the council of municipalities who happened to be my friend, I asked that Goran be sent since he was in Novi Sad, and he arrived in my home with two more people in the car. Since he didn't dare enter the house, he wanted to go to Pacetina to talk to me there and so we did. I explained to him why I wanted him there, and I asked him to leave the person alone and not to have him removed since he worked on some organisational aspects. He said that he held nothing against the person in question but that Milosevic had a problem with him and that that's why he was being removed. To tell you the truth, I neither kept any record of any meetings nor was there any need to do that. And this transpired the way I just explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who the person in question was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, why not? Boro Drzajic, president of the Executive Council. There was a Regional Council at the time for the area of Vukovar, Dalj, Mirkovci, and other places. That's what it's all about. Oh, sorry, it wasn't 1995. That was later. That was just before the peacekeeping forces arrived. Until 1995, I'm not sure. I didn't really think about that much, and there was -- there wasn't any need to. We didn't have any proper contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll put something to you in brief, hoping to encompass everything that's in your statement regarding that. I will put to you 18 points that we assert are incorrect in your statement. I'll enumerate them, and then we'll go back to each one of them. First of all, that you appointed Goran Hadzic president of the SDS board in Vukovar and that later on you backed him, as you said. That's paragraphs 7 and 23 of your statement. Next, that you provided or issued tasks to Vukcevic and Hadzic, which is what you say in paragraph 12 regarding a meeting in Knin where Professor Raskovic was under verbal attack. Thirdly, that Goran Hadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Where Mr. Raskovic was attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Then in paragraph 1, that Goran Hadzic had some personal interest in being in Belgrade. Number four, that Goran Hadzic, on the day when he was released from gaol in Zagreb or, rather, the hospital, called Ilija Koncarevic on the phone, which is paragraph 70 of your statement. Next, that Goran Hadzic provided legitimacy to those who engaged in looting, which is also in paragraph 70. And that you ever discussed Arkan with him, which is also paragraph 70. Next, item 7, that Lazar Sarac was ever Goran Hadzic's bodyguard as you state in paragraph 78. Eight, that Goran Hadzic ever received 50 side -- pieces of sidearms from Trifunovic [as interpreted], whom you otherwise termed a provocateur, which is in paragraph 80 of your statement. And you repeated that yesterday, page 70, line 25 of yesterday's transcript. Number nine, that Hadzic told you that he was on his way to Belgrade because of Milosevic. That is paragraph 82. Number ten, that he publicly advocated the creation of a Serbian state in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srijem. This is paragraph 85. Number 11, that Dusan Pekic was his advisor. That's paragraph 131. Number 12, that any meeting of the government of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srijem was ever held in Belgrade. That is also in paragraph 131. Number 13, that General Pekic supplied Hadzic with weapons. This is paragraph 133. Number 14, that at the 30th of October, 1991, meeting, the moving of the civilian population from Lovas was discussed. This is paragraph 150 of your statement. Number 15, that Stevo Bogic was subordinated to Goran Hadzic and that he was head of the State Security Service. This is paragraph 183. Number 16, that Goran Hadzic knew about the minefield incident at Lovas, that he had ever been to Lovas and that he had ever met you there. This is paragraph 183. Number 17, that Goran Hadzic did nothing about protecting the non-Serb population of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srijem. This is paragraph 193. And number 18, that Goran Hadzic was in charge of creating conflict in Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srijem.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please repeat the name of the author of the book. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, the interpreter has asked that you repeat the name of the author of the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The name of the author is Josip Boljkovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: We didn't also get the paragraph number for number 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is paragraph 196.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me start with the last thing that we spoke about. I'd like you to look at an exhibit provided by the OTP. This is 2786. You see the document there, don't you? Perhaps we should zoom in, or perhaps I could read it back to you. The text is in the Croatian language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No need for you to read it back to me. I'm familiar with the substance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's first try to shed some light on this. Up until July 1991, Josip Boljkovac served as the interior minister of Croatia. Do you agree with me, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This piece was published in "Vecernji List" on the 30th of May, 2011. "Vecernji List" is a Croatian daily published in Zagreb; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The headline reads -- it's a quote from Josip Boljkovac, who says: "Goran Hadzic was a peacemaker. He collaborated or co-operated back in 1991." You saw the piece, and you read the piece, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I'm sorry, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You need to answer out loud.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry, I just wasn't looking at you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In this piece he said, among other things, just to avoid going through the whole thing, that Goran Hadzic was in charge of peacemaking. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This was said at one time in some context or other. Mr. Boljkovac and I are on very good terms. I always go and see him when I have time. And this goes back to the time when he picked us up from the Sveto Simunska hospital. When he came to get us there. So this was the first time we met, and we immediately hit it off. He was a very special person in Franjo Tudjman's first government. He was the interior minister. There were all these problems, and there were all these things that needed doing, and he was adamant that everything should be done in a peaceful way. Back in his ministry, he even had some people there who were Franjo Tudjman's Trojan horses, so to speak, including the deputy minister himself. I've had such interesting conversations with him over time that I'm always glad, because he speaks up for the Croats, and I speak up for the Serbs. And this is just a perfect reflection of my position. It's the Croats who should be addressing the Croat issue and the Serbs who should be addressing the Serb issue in turn, if we want to tackle any issue at all. So that was the situation, and I can't remember the exact cause, what triggered the situation or indeed the statement that he made for this daily. He probably felt the need to say it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Are his words truthful? Was he speaking the truth here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It really depends on the moment. It's difficult for me to say whether he told the truth, and it's also about how the words were conveyed by the journalists. It's a matter of the moment. I have no reason to doubt his good intentions. I have no reason to doubt his judgement. There were other statements that were made on various occasions for different reasons, you know, that sort of thing, but this got written up the way that we see it, you know, and I can do nothing else but simply to agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But the point of my question is not the way it was written up, because we can see for ourselves, can't we? This is something that Mr. Boljkovac is quoted as saying. Is that truthful, the substance of the quote attributed to him, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I hardly put myself in a position to judge any statement that he may have made.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You just said something about him advocating a peaceful solution for any conflicts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, I notice that you are quoting the title of this document or article, whatever, but in the quote you just mentioned, the quote of the person saying this, it is not only said that Goran Hadzic was nothing but a peacemaker, but it's specified at the beginning of the war in Croatia. So I would like to have that in the quote when you ask the question to the witness. It might assist his interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't finish with this document. I have more question for him. But the year 1991 indicates that it was at the very start of the war, or the period before the beginning of the war and the first month of the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I'm sorry that I intervened, Mr. Zivanovic, but I did because you specifically mentioned the quote.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And then the quote was not correct in -- well, I thought -- I don't say it was not correct. It was not complete. Because the title of an article is always different from the article itself, and the title of a quote is the same. So I apologise for intervening.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I do not -- I have no intent to mislead the witness or anyone here, but the title says: "Boljkovac: Goran Hadzic was peacemaker. He co-operated in 1991."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Before we return to this document, I just wanted to ask you one thing. You say that Mr. Boljkovac was in favour of a peaceful solution. He was the interior minister at the time. Was he one of the few in Croatia's government back then who was, in fact, advocating a peaceful solution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: More like the only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If you read on, it says that Goran Hadzic attended numerous meetings where a peaceful solution was being arranged, and Mr. Boljkovac himself attended those as well. Are you familiar with that, the fact that these meetings were held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If he said so, then I'm sure they were. As for the exact date or place, I don't have access to that information, but if Boljkovac said this, then I have no doubt that it's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: He mentioned Vukovar, Vinkovci, Obrovac, Backa Palanka, but okay, you say you know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Boljkovac was not at Obrovac, we were. Backa Palanka, I don't believe, frankly, that any of us were there. As for Vukovar, I think it was the day that we were driven over from the prison hospital. They dropped me home, and they had a meeting after that. But if -- if he's the person saying this, then I definitely agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just below the headline you see what it says. When Tudjman and Milosevic rejected a peaceful solution, Hadzic's line was quashed and war began, says the former minister.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Tudjman and Milosevic had great respect for their advisors. So Milosevic's advisors were all well regarded by Tudjman, and this cut both ways. Mr. Boljkovac was removed or dismissed at the request of Slobodan Milosevic. Tudjman fired him, and then Boljkovac wanted some sort of reasoning to be presented for his dismissal, and Tudjman simply told him, "Slobodan does not agree with you being there. He doesn't like you being there." And this is something that Mr. Boljkovac shared with me personally. I have no reason to doubt his openness. So anyone who was in Milosevic's good books automatically qualified with Tudjman as well, because they really respected each other, and they co-ordinated everything between Zagreb and Belgrade, which after all is a well-known fact these days. Some people know more about it, some people not so much, but that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Believe me, I myself had no idea that Tudjman was in a position to affect any personnel decisions made by Milosevic or indeed vice versa. Frankly, I find the assertion slightly outlandish, especially on the eve of a major war.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Savic, the interpreter's asked would you repeat the answer, the last answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What exactly is this in reference to?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I said that I had no idea how Milosevic could possibly affect any personnel-related decisions between Tudjman and vice versa, since we know that these two were diametrically opposed and finally started fighting, entered a war.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and I said they had a great deal of respect for each other, and that their associates were always well regarded on both sides of the divide. As for them fighting to any great extent, well, I think that is a matter for future debate, frankly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir. What do you mean "fighting to any great extent"? My impression is it was quite a fierce clash over the four years that it took.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let's try and name a single battle where these two actually clashed. All the acts of provocation occurring across the country were well organised and well under control. Look at the footage. Go ahead. Find something where you encounter a real war atmosphere. This is mere propaganda if you look at it. If you look at all that footage of the Home Guard on the Croatian side, can you actually see any Croatian soldiers in that footage? Come on. Or Operation Storm. Have you seen footage of that? They're shooting bullets up into the air, and there's celebratory fire, but do you have any footage of actual fighting? Do you have any footage of the -- the other side, the enemy? You know what I'm talking about. So if you really apply yourself, if you analyse the whole thing closely, then we should probably give a different name to it. Large-scale war, hmm. Victims, yes, there were some victims, as a matter of fact, but it was all an organised thing. It was staged. So it's -- it's not like there was any great degree of hostility between Milosevic and Tudjman that erupted in the form of a war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't have in mind their personal relationship. They may well have had one, but their political positions, even though you may not agree, were diametrically opposed when it comes to resolving the crisis in the then Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were discussing their staff and the mutual respect they had for each other's advisors. Let's take Sarinic. He went to Belgrade numerous times. He was a very close associate of President Tudjman, and for a while he was his chef de cabinet. There were many other contacts that were not registered anywhere. There was a lively communication in terms of exchanging information and arranging their associates. It just wasn't discussed. I'm not putting that in a negative context. I'm simply stating that. It was normal, of course, to keep in touch, to be in contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I find it hard to understand that, as you say, there was a lot of footage which only served as propaganda, as PR, if you will. I am mindful of the images of Vukovar which certainly could not be used as any kind of commercial, so to say. That's why I'm surprised by your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was propaganda for those who were engaged in destruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's conclude with this exhibit. In this article Goran Hadzic -- Mr. Boljkovac states that Goran Hadzic joined the Milosevic line, the Serb line, and that he took part in the conflict. He also asserts that it is correct that he was indicted before the International Tribunal and that he's still on the run. You read the article, and you agree with that. It's not that he only talked about Hadzic as a -- as a man who was in favour of peace all along.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I agree. There's a shift of position.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement, in paragraph 196 you mentioned a book. You said that Boljkovac, in that book, wrote that Goran Hadzic was the kind of person who created conflict in Slavonia, Baranja and Western Sirmium and that you find it to be correct. It's paragraph 196. Let me ask you this first: Which book is it? Can you tell us where Mr. Boljkovac wrote that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the title is the "The Truth Must Out," [as interpreted] where he describes all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we next have a look at 1D2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I apologise. The previous article was introduced by Mr. Zivanovic as an exhibit, but it's actually only a 65 ter. It's only on our 65 ter list. So it's not an exhibit. So if Mr. Zivanovic wants to tender it, it would be the appropriate moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We will ask to tender this exhibit, although I don't know if it is on the Prosecution list of exhibits, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. It's at tab 46 of our list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So you ask to tender it, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked as a Defence -- is it -- as a Defence exhibit then, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit Number D4. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us have a look at the book by Mr. Boljkovac next. It is already in e-court, but I also have it in hard copy if that would be easier for you. Let's try and make this exercise easier. I presume you don't know off-the-cuff where that piece of text is in the book that you mentioned in your statement. I'll try to make things easier for you. At the end of the book, I think it is the very last page of this document --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, do we have a translation for this book, for the excerpts you wish to show, because we haven't been provided them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just certain pages of this book are translated because the book is 200 pages long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, the Registrar tells me that the translations are not available in e-court. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. We ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We -- we submitted this translation, and I think that we have it here. Just a moment, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, perhaps I could propose -- I'm looking at the time. Could you -- could you address your next item - I suppose it's number 16 of your 18 points - and figure this out during the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Would that be appropriate?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It seems that the translation appear -- is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: That's the translation of the previous document that was just --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday, you testified about going to Sid, which is pages 84 and 85 of the transcript. You said that before going there, you were in contact with Colonel Djokovic, I believe, from the military security service, and that he had given you a Scorpion gun. Do state your answer clearly, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Based on evidence we have here concerning your trip, which is number 341 on the Prosecution list --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Which is now Exhibit P77.50. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is stated on page 4 in our language and page 3 in the English translation that upon your arrival in Sid on the 29th of September, 1991, you were authorised by the TO Vukovar Chief of Staff Grahovac to assemble volunteers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: One page before that in the Serbian version, which in the English translation it is pages 2 and 3, it is stated that Grahovac also approved that you can carry M-56, an automatic weapon, for your personal safety, and we even have the number of the weapon mentioned. I'm interested in why you wanted this M-56 if you had already had the Scorpion provided by Colonel Djokovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because Mr. Grahovac insisted. He said, Take this. I don't know whether I had the Scorpion with me, because I don't usually bear arms. It may have been in my car, but I really don't know. And I said, Fine. Issue me -- issue a licence for me, and I'll take it. There was no particular reason. He just said, Well, this is just in case you should be stopped. It's better to have a weapon with you. So there was nothing special about the arrangement. I didn't carry either of the two, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you tell him that you already had an automatic weapon and that you did not need another one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm telling you, it's not that I wanted it. He insisted. I think I left the Scorpion back home in Sabac. It wasn't important to me. He gave me the papers, and I put it in the car. Others did not even get any papers from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to the documents we have, I can see you were given a licence to carry the Scorpion, but it happened only later, in 1992, and not when you went to Sid.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I agree with the date on the licence. I agree fully. You know, you can't keep it all in your memory, the date, the period, but it tallies with the sequence of events. I think it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the last page of the document in both versions. We can see it in the Serbian language. Could we scroll up in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: It's the page before in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. [Interpretation] Yes. We'll look at the previous page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You see, here we see why the licence was issued. Not just anyone could receive a Scorpion gun. It's not something a citizen could carry around.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It says here that the licence was issued pursuant to an order of the TO commander of the Republic of Serbia and that the order was strictly confidential.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djokic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is also stated that the order was issued on the 27th of August, 1991, and you were provided with the licence for the period between the 20th of February and the 20th of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So that does not tally with what you told us about receiving the Scorpion gun from Colonel Djokovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think this is Djokovic's signature. Yes. Djokovic and Djokic is similar, but I think this is Djokovic's signature. As regards the licence, obviously they assign me some sort of higher level or rank. I told you I didn't ask for such weapon. I only wanted a licence, and this is the only one. I didn't even read the licence. I wasn't interested. He issued it. He signed it. There's nothing to discuss.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in this: Did you get the weapon in September 1991 or in February 1992? That's the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The answer is this: I received it on the date of the licence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Hence I conclude that in September 1991 or October 1991, you did not get a Scorpion gun from Djokovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if we go by the date, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's time for the break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Savic, we will take the first break now. We will return at 11.00. You will be escorted out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Savic, let us now return to that book. We ran out of time during the previous session, so I'll be showing it to you now. This is Exhibit 1D2, and that's Mr. Boljkovac's book that we were talking about. Just to say this again, you say that in that book Mr. Boljkovac talks about Goran Hadzic as being a person who created conflict in Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srijem, and you believe that to be true. Let us go back to that book. We'll not go through all of its pages and it's very difficult to pinpoint the exact spot where he talks about that, but I would like us to go to page 10 in e-court, which is the very final part of the book. Why is that important? Because we have a list of names there. It's a glossary of names mentioned in the book, and we'll find there the exact reference to Goran Hadzic, the page number and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's not translated, but I think it is not necessary, because it contains only first and last names of the persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Is it the one we have on the screen now? Is it that page?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That's what I thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We need -- in B/C/S version it is page 10. It is register of names. We shall go two page -- two pages to the letter H. Next page, I think. Yes. I think that we are here.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is page 14, for the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this is the list of names mentioned in the book with the appropriate page references, and you can see where Mr. Hadzic's name crops up in the book, the letter H. His name is mentioned in two places, page 230 and page 235. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we now please go to page 230 to check the reference. In the English, this is page 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And for the record, the name of the book is "The Truth Must Come Out." I noticed that in the transcript there was another name, "The Truth Must Be Told," I think, but it is "The Truth Must Come Out."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is page 230, page 12 in the English translation. Do you see the context in which reference is made to your name and Mr. Hadzic's name? Mr. Boljkovac talks about the arrest of you and Goran Hadzic. The names are only mentioned in the heading. The next page is 235. That's two pages on. The English is page 23 through page 25. I think that's correct. Mr. Boljkovac talks about Goran Hadzic here. Perhaps we could read this portion. It's not really that long. He says: "The very controversial case of Goran Hadzic, a man wanted by The Hague, and at one time the leading figure in the Krajina parastate is also linked to the events in Plitvice. The above-mentioned meeting in Obrovac was in fact attended by Hadzic, the then-member of the Executive Board of the Serbian Democratic Party, and Borivoje Savic, the secretary of that party's Vukovar branch. At the time, they advocated a more moderate option, which is borne out by the fact that over the course of those weeks they were part of the Serbian delegation which was in Zagreb for talks with Tudjman. My deputy, Degoricija, was in contact with both of them during that period and was trying to improve collaboration. My deputy even gave Hadzic an official pistol. Degoricija was convinced that in this way he had succeeded in getting to the very top echelons of the Serbian rebel hornets' nest with his tentacles which, however, proved to be a delusion. "As chance would have it, when these two men were returning from Obrovac on Easter night, they actually stayed at the Plitvice hotel. They were among those arrested in the morning and were badly beaten because of the pistol that Hadzic had on them, since the policemen treated them as rebels. They mentioned Degoricija, but the policemen took this to be an additional act of provocation. They spent a brief period in hospital because of their injuries. It was only once we had been informed of the arrest that the two men were released and subsequently returned to Vukovar. "I established contact with them in April before I left for a meeting with the Serbian minister of internal affairs, Radmilo Bogdanovic, in Backa Palanka. We also attended some meetings with representatives of the Serbian community in Vukovar and Vinkovci, where I was adamant that we should strengthen the inter-ethnic dialogue. "The denouement of Hadzic's story is well known. Contrary to Savic, who lives in Croatia to this day, the bearded warehouseman from Pacetina took special care to dispel any suspicion that he had actually been in contact with the Croatian MUP up until the time of the carnage in Borovo Selo. He provided proof of his suddenly resurgent radicalism in 1992 through 1993, when he assumed the position of president of the self-proclaimed 'Serbian Republic of Krajina.' As a war crimes suspect, he was on The Hague Tribunal's wanted list, but continued to live peacefully in Vojvodina for years. He disappeared after the Serbian authorities themselves informed him that he would be arrested after all, so justice has not yet been done." Having read this, do you notice any references by Mr. Boljkovac in this portion to Goran Hadzic as being the person who stirred up conflict in Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srijem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The text itself contains a number of imprecisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But I'd like to take you back one step. I'd like to take you back to your own statement in paragraph 196 where you say that in his book, Boljkovac says that Goran Hadzic was the person who created conflict in Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srijem. I showed you the relevant portions of the book where Goran Hadzic's name appears. Have you come across any references in the relevant portions to Goran Hadzic as a person who created conflict in Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srijem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But if you analyse the text itself, you can arrive at that conclusion as well, can't you, the very beginning of that portion, and then later on in the text suspicions like that might crop up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Suspicion is one thing, but what you state is that he actually wrote that. It is up to you to interpret this any way you like. Nevertheless, in your statement you claim that Boljkovac in writing actually described Goran Hadzic as a person who created conflict in Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srijem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In one of the interviews in the written media and there was a TV show as well where Boljkovac actually said this. I don't remember how specific I was, whether indeed I said that he wrote this in his book. Nonetheless, there are published articles and pieces containing statements that he made to precisely that effect. I'm not sure I said he wrote this in his book. The text itself is quite imprecise.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, please wait for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We'll read another even shorter portion from Mr. Boljkovac's book. This is at page 238. That's two pages on from the page we were looking at. In the English, that is page 26. It reads: "The -- it was in fact during those months that the type of provocations carried out by the Serbian extremists in the territory of the Krajina municipalities were mirrored on the other side in the events which occurred in Slavonia. There were frequent incidents in the field, which, according to information I had at the time, were mostly provoked by the Croatian side." Based on that, my impression is Mr. Boljkovac was actually quite specific when he talked about the incidents in Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srijem which led to the clashes that eventually erupted, and it is not my impression that he mentioned Goran Hadzic as being a person who created conflict, as you suggested, in Slavonia and Baranja. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Was I speaking about the co-ordination between Belgrade and Zagreb in relation to those incidents? I think I actually mentioned that. Co-ordination was there. That much is certain. One act of provocation is stoked up by both of the sides involved in a manner of speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I think you explained something to the effect that there was some agreements between the two sides.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's where it's at. That's where you find the initiators as well as those involved, maybe not by name, but we did speak about the co-operation between Milosevic and Tudjman, didn't we. We spoke about the persons who worked with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. I would now like to pick up where we left off before the break. So if we look at these documents, what follows is that on the 29th of September, you arrived in Sid. You met Slobodan Grahovac, and you obtained from him a permit to carry firearms, and he also tasked you with something on that occasion. This is 341, OTP Exhibit 341.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I would just tender this exhibit, previous exhibit into evidence. It is 1D2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It should be assigned Exhibit Number D5. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just to jog our memories, the 29th of September, 1991, you received permission from Slobodan Grahovac to gather volunteers, and you were also granted a permit to carry an M-56; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what was happening, for example, on the 29th of September in those areas, the area where you happened to be at the time in Sid? Can you remember that? Not necessarily that same day, but the next day and that general time-frame.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The area around Sid was teeming with soldiers all the way from Bacinci, which is not far from Sid, Vukojevci, and then along the road to Bajakovo, as well as the town itself. There were quite many volunteers in the town itself. It was difficult to say which unit they belonged to. There were all sorts there. The town was full. And there were all these staff activities registering people and dispatching them to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You probably know that it was on at that day that the 1st Guards Brigade of the JNA headed towards Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was on that same day but the Guards Brigade did not arrive from that direction. The Guards Brigade, I think, came across the Danube. Actually, I'm speculating. Actually, I don't really know which direction they came from, but it is possible that what you say is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, you didn't see them or you have no knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This authorisation to assemble volunteers was provided to you on the 29th of September, 1991, and it is clear that it was to be in force for a month until the 30th of October. If you wish me to show it to you, we can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I'll take your word for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So that is Exhibit 341, page 4 in the Serbian version and 3 in the English. We have already seen that. According to my information, you arrived in Lovas on the 23rd of October. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to that information, and you did discuss that in paragraphs 152 through 155, there were volunteers there already from the Dusan Silni Detachment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you got in touch with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What was the nature of your communication with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A very good one. I asked them simply to conduct properly while they were in the village irrespective of whether they had done anything previously. I asked them to assist if there is any need and to stay near their places of accommodation. There were no particular problems with them. I asked them who had brought them there. They said Aca Vasiljevic had, without me insisting on any names. So I asked them who brought them, and they said Aleksandar Vasiljevic did. Throughout my stay there, we would meet when I happened to be in the village, although there were no particular tasks or duties to attend to. In any case, I met with them on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Who did they receive their orders from, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't say. There were no particular orders. Once Mirko Jovic was there with another man. I don't know what was the nature of their communication on that occasion, but he was there once. I didn't see him afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Some exhibits that were shown to you, which you have as well, include minutes taken by you. In particular, it is number 498 on the Prosecution list. The minutes in question are dated the 30th of October, 1991. You are designated as the person taking the minutes in the document itself. It means that the minutes were drafted by you; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: There is a list of attendees on behalf of the government, as you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That's how they introduced themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I can see here that you assigned certain positions to the attendees which were not the positions they held according to a decision that was made on the members of government for Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Sirmium, which is Prosecutor's 322.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can you point out the errors?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The first person is Vitomir Devetak. You mention him as the president of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we don't find it there, but Vitomir Devetak was a government minister in charge of the war economy. If we go back to that decision number 322, we find his name under number 4.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can see it. What I know is that he was the president of the SDS board in Borovo Selo. I didn't know that he was the minister of war economy. It seems to be my mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The next person is Stevo Bogic, aka Jajo, deputy prime minister and state security chief according to your minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the decision published in the Official Gazette of the Serbian district we read that Stevo Bogic was the minister with that portfolio.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When was the decision issued?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 25th of September. So a month before this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It seems, then, that I assigned him a more senior position than he actually held, but in any case, I agree. I don't think it's a major mistake or omission, though. The fact is that he was in attendance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see, this is the cover page of the minutes. Did you keep minutes for the entire session?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I noted each and every contribution, but here at the beginning I simply wanted to list those in attendance and the agenda as well. The agenda was under number 1, political and security situation, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We can see that. There's no need to read it out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Yesterday, I did touch upon this. The key item was number 2, economical, agricultural problems. Members or presidents of municipalities and local communes were consulted in terms of the autumn season and production of raw materials. That was the key issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you spoke to the investigators of the OTP, did you tell them that the minutes contained -- contain more than one page? You actually kept notes of the entire meeting. This is only the first page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did explain that, and I explained how the meeting was called, as well as the topics discussed. You see, this was typed on a computer. We did not have a typewriter. Actually, at the time, I did it all in handwriting, and instead of copying it all because there wasn't -- there were things that were not so important, I explained it the way I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And where are the other pages of the minutes? Why did you not provide them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have them. I can send them, no problem. I can send them to your office.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Weren't you asked then to provide the entire minutes rather than just the first page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, no, I wasn't. And there didn't seem to be a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Savic, we got hold of another version of minutes from the same meeting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was produced by the army, wasn't it? There was someone from the armed forces or actually a local commune employee who did it on their behalf; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was about to show it to you, so you can tell us whether that is the case. It is 1D8.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. If I may be allowed to comment upon both minutes. The first set of minutes accuses no one. Any of the notes that I took down. This is how minutes were kept, but there were also secret minutes kept by those who were in charge of operations. That may be the only difference. In any case, all those in attendance were free to take their own notes or minutes. It was not prohibited. People did the way they chose to in that session. The one I produced -- actually, these minutes here were made for a certain purpose, and I know how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that the first set of minutes accuses no one, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had in mind the first set of minutes which I delivered. It was simply a way to note down that there was a meeting, and I explained it, and there's nothing to discuss any further. This set of minutes or any other that may be in existence, that's another thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But you did not forward the entire minutes, only the first page, as you say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I showed them the document. If anyone needs anything on top of that, I'm free -- I'm willing to have it delivered, no problem. I simply wanted to register that there was a meeting. If anything else is necessary, I will gladly provide it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You say you showed it to them. You mean the Prosecutor's office when they interviewed you, or someone else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I showed it to them? What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said, "I showed them the document." That's in the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could I have that interpreted, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe they will interpret that for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I still did not hear it. I'm not receiving anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: There's some technical problem. To repeat my question. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that the first document accused no one, and that was the basis for my question. You said you forwarded the minutes, but I simply noted that it was only the first page, and then you said you showed it to them. Who is "them," the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I showed them the minutes. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you who did you show it to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Prosecutor's office, because you received it from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So you say you only handed over that one page; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Which means that we couldn't get the transcript of the minutes in its entirety; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never handed over a handwritten set of minutes. I was only referring to the one page that I did hand over.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. I understand that. You suggest that the minutes you were shown were kept by the military; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the purposes of the military, by one of the officials of the Lovas local community.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So there are these minutes and the fact that the minutes were kept by military, yet you make absolutely no reference to this in your statement; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No one asked. We just never ended up discussing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: These are handwritten minutes, which makes it -- the document very difficult to read. Nevertheless, the Translation Unit appears to have done a very good job. They even provide a translation. We'll go through it to check for errors. Nevertheless, I won't be asking you about the substance of the minutes. I'll be asking you to look at the penultimate page of the minutes. The English reference is page 13. I'm looking at the English translation. Near the top I can see that some text is missing. Now I'm looking at the Serbian and it reads: "A meeting of representatives of the villages and government at Lovas," followed by the date. Do you agree, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You see what is quite noteworthy for our purposes is the Serbian text. I see all these handwritten entries, the names of those attending the meeting. That's the column on the left-hand side followed by another column, the place they hail from; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Followed by yet another column containing their official capacity, position; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: There's no need to go through each and every one of these individual names. Rather, I'd like us to go to the next page, which I think is the final page of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Number 25. That's your name; right? Borivoje Savic. Place, Lovas. And then it reads "Member of the TO staff." The Territorial Defence Staff; right? Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Based on what I've seen here, I can infer that each of these persons just put their own names on this list in their own handwriting; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. And my signature is there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It says "Lovas," and it says "TO staff member." I think you wrote that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Truth to tell, I can't be absolutely certain whether I was the one who wrote those words there. Nonetheless, I wasn't trying to appear to hold an office of greater importance rather than just being a member of the TO staff. So I can hardly believe this. Who wrote this? Why did they write it like this? But I don't see a thorny issue here. I was no staff member. That much is certain. Nor did I ever describe myself as one. I'm trying to think back. There was a contact person, but I myself was not involved in the staff's work or indeed linked to the staff at all. Not that the staff was necessarily involved in the specific activities apart from making occasional appointments. I'm not really aware of any hands-on activities that they pursued at all. In the Lovas area, there were no actions and no movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, you are not in a position to confirm that the portion of text that follows your name, meaning the place and the title or official capacity, where it says "Lovas," and then it says "TO staff member," you cannot confirm that you wrote that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Where it says "TO staff member," that's not my handwriting. I'm sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But you see, I'm no handwriting expert. If at any point that is indeed required, we can enlist the assistance of one. But I'm looking at all the other persons -- the names signed in this document. For example, number 23. My impression is that the handwriting is the same where the name is written, where the place is written, and where the official capacity or position is written. Same handwriting throughout, in other words. Likewise number 24. But now you are trying to tell us that it is not the case with your own number. Yet again, if we move on to number 26, the same pattern emerges, the same handwriting throughout across the three columns. 27, 28, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is tendentious, the way you're putting it. It has nothing to do with it. It's not that I was afraid of anything or indeed trying to hide anything. It wouldn't be a problem for me to own up if that indeed were the case, but it's not, you know. If that is the greatest problem that we have here, I might as well say yes, you're right, but it's not necessarily that I consider this to be a major wrongdoing or a major sin. It might be a instance of manipulation, yes. But what is this? It is set of minutes. They were kept just like that. I signed this because it was put in front of me. TO staff member, nothing to do with anything at all. I would never have agreed to become a staff member of any kind.
