Although even that, even that, what would have been wrong with that if you just stop a minute to ponder the possibility? What? So that's why. You see what I'm trying to say. How was this used? You know, that arouses my suspicion. It's not about me. I'm not the problem here. Will you choose to believe that I was a staff member or not, well, that's up to each of us individually; right? But it's not something that bears any relevance at all to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. I think it's up to the Trial Chamber to judge the relevance, but if we link this up with the other document showing you to be in the Territorial Defence Staff in Sid, this might after all prove to be interconnected, you see.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Well, I don't know. I can't say, can I. I don't think there's anything about this that can be challenged. This is an area with paramilitary activity, and there were no official positions, really. So if you're talking about the posting itself, okay, you can have it. I don't care. It's not that I'm bothered by this. There is someone who believes that I was a member of this staff. I can provide an additional explanation if you think this is something that is cumbersome, but the one thing that I'm telling you is that the handwriting here is not mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You say you were communicating with these people, the members of the Dusan Silni Detachment in Lovas; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is paragraph -- just a minute, please. Paragraph 152 through 155 of your statement. I think you also suggest that you warned them. You said something about not having any of it, them causing an incident. They were to behave, something like that; right? Did they actually follow your instructions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Well, this is only about the period of time they spent with me. Aside from that, when they were outside my purview, so to speak, how was I to be responsible for anybody's actions, you see?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What was the exact time period that they were with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the time I arrived and then the following 20 days until I left, but they were there throughout, and they stayed after I'd left.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just tell me one thing, please. Did you have any information suggesting that they were not behaving properly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were complaints about a man named Kosta. I'm not sure about his surname. People were complaining about him. I think he even killed someone. I'm not sure who, whether it was a man or a woman, but it -- he was trouble. The other lads there were quite fair. They were all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Based on my information, you gave evidence at the Higher Court in Belgrade in the Lovas case, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we have 1D6, please. Sorry, Your Honours, I have forgot again to ask admitting into evidence the previous document. It is 1D8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit Number D6. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that trial, you appeared as a Defence witness for the two accused; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You say that you arrived in Lovas on the 23rd of October, that evening, that is. The reference is pages 3 through 7 in the Serbian and pages 3 through 9 in the English. Ten days previously, you had gone to see General Simic. The Serbian reference is page 7, and page 9 in the English. He refused to talk to you. Djordje Ivkovic came with you, who was for a while the SUP head in Vukovar. That's page 8 in the Serbian and page 10 in the English. When he came there, you found some volunteers. You showed them into your office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Among them was a man named Zoran Obrenovic, also known as Azdaja.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's page 10 in the Serbian and page 13 for the English. You say there were soldiers all over Lovas. Page 12 in the Serbian and page 15 in the English. You say you had a permit from Belgrade. Again, page 12, Serbian; page 16, English. The day before the meeting took place on the 30th of September, you saw Arkan. That's page 13 Serbian, and page 17, English. The 30th of September. You also drew up an agenda for the meeting, and you kept your own minutes. You were then told that the minutes were kept by Pavle Klisuric, a local from Lovas; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that the staff at Sid was set up in October. That's page 15 Serbian, page 19 English. The staff commander was Dusan Filipovic. 15 Serbian, 20 English. The staff was headed by Slobodan Grahovac. Grahovac was assigned as jureske [phoen] for a while in 1992. That's also what you said. You said you were there because you were making a sacrifice. 16 Serbian, 21 English. You say you were given a permanent permit at the Central Committee building and this was arranged for you by an acquaintance from Osijek, Nikola Kaloper. Page 17 in the Serbian and page 23 in the English. General Nenezic told you that the army had kicked up a shit storm in Lovas. That's 18 in the Serbian and 23 in the English. Zoran Obrenovic, aka Azdaja, was particularly attached to you and he followed you all over. Page 21 in the Serbian and page 27 in the English. You don't know what the volunteers were doing in Lovas. Page 22 in both versions of the text. You said you carried a Scorpio. Page 23 in the Serbian and page 29 in the English. You said the volunteers were from the Dusan Silni Detachment. Page 23 in the English and page 31 -- page 23 in the Serbian and page 31 in the English. You also said that you were given a TT weapon by Nikola Kaloper. Page 29 in the one version and page 30 in the other. And you admitted that you signed the minutes that you were shown. I quoted this in a bid to avoid reading the minutes in their entirety, but is my rendition accurate, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have one addition to make. We did not go to see Arkan. The day before our departure for Erdut, we were on our way to Novi Sad to see Mr. Hadzic at his place. Ljuban went there to pick him up, but he had taken cover because he wasn't willing to travel to Erdut. That at least was our inference, because we had agreed for him to wait up there. And then we pressed on for Erdut. We were there in a government office. I can't remember who was there, what specific government members. I recommend that Gogic was there. And then at one point in time, Ljuban told me that they were on their way to the kitchen downstairs because Arkan was there. It's actually a room outside the government building, and he said, You stay here and talk to Jajo. So they left and Jajo and I were now alone in the office. And then he goes, Okay, so you're one of us; right? And I say, Is this supposed to be some sort of conversation between us? And he said, Yeah, and what were you thinking? And I said, You stupid git. Don't you know that nothing has changed between us, and I left the room. Outside there were two of Arkan's Men waiting, and they saw me over to the kitchen where Arkan was with a friend of mine who exerted quite some influence on Arkan, but it was nothing to do with the meeting, because everything had been agreed upstairs at the meeting. So Arkan was there and it was a matter of protocol of some kind to go there and see him since they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You just mentioned Goran Hadzic. So you went there to see him, but you didn't actually end up seeing him. Are you trying to suggest that he avoided seeing you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was Ljuban Devetak who arranged the whole thing. We arrived in Novi Sad. We got to his flat. Ljuban had 15.000 dinars for him. He went up to his flat. He left the money there, but he said, He's out. He's probably run away. So there you go.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can I ask 1D6 to be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked. Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. Just -- does counsel want to enter the entire testimony of Mr. Savic in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: All right. Your Honours, I'm not entirely sure how this works. We already have the witness's 92 ter statement in evidence, and counsel did elicit a number of questions out of the testimony. I don't know if we're circumventing some of the rules by tendering the entire testimony of the witness before another court. I think the answers are in the transcript. I don't know whether the whole testimony needs to go in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, this testimony is much longer than the parts you were discussing with the witness; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours. I went through whole relevant issues with him during this cross-examination, but I think that it would be good for the Trial Chamber to have entirety of this testimony, to see it. It would be -- it would be useful in my -- in my view, and it is used for the purpose of impeachment also so that --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I just add one more thing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: The witness has not been given the chance to review this transcript and to verify the accuracy, and the transcript that we have is 38 pages. My learned friend has read maybe about ten excerpts out of it, so we don't know what else there is in there, whether the witness actually confirms that everything in there is accurately transcribed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, I have another concern. If I understand your answer to the -- your last answer to the President correctly, when you were talking about the entirety of that transcript, portions of which you have put to the witness, being useful for the possibility of impeaching him, the implication of that is that over and apart from such items as you would have identified by putting questions to him and eliciting answers, the implication is that the Chamber would itself go into portions of the document and, to add to what Mr. Demirdjian has -- to what Mr. Demirdjian has said, it's a document which the rest of it the witness hasn't necessarily taken on board and then the Chamber itself would use it to challenge the credibility of the witness. I have a problem with that. Did I misunderstand your suggestion?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very simply, I think that entirety of this particular testimony of the witness before War Chamber of the Belgrade court may assist the Chamber in assessment of credibility of the testimony of the witness before this Chamber. It was only purpose, because for my -- for my proposal to admit this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber -- yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I apologise for intervening, Mr. President. It's just to add, not with respect to this specific transcript, but the Trial Chamber's probably going to learn that there are proceedings that occurred in Belgrade and in Osijek involving various events that are part of -- in -- that are charged in the indictment in this case, and so I just wanted to mention, I think it's -- whatever approach the Chamber decides to take on this issue, it's probably one that could recur, because there is actually a lot of overlap between this trial and proceedings that have already occurred either in Belgrade or in Osijek.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber is of the view that it cannot admit the entirety of this testimony into evidence, and we will stick to what is on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Savic, I will now take you back to your statement, paragraph 70. There, among other things, you say that you broke off your relationship with Hadzic the day you left the prison hospital in Zagreb and when you heard that allegedly he spoke on the phone with Ilija Koncarevic. Among other things, you asked him why he was around people like Arkan. My question is this: Did you ask him that question then, why he was around people like Arkan en route back from Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pardon me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Zivanovic. I'll come back to the previous issue when you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Sorry. Just one moment. I'm pushing the -- I'm pushing the wrong button. Sorry about that. Mr. Zivanovic, what I said was, so now it's on the record, that you may proceed, and that I'll come back to the previous issue in between two questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So my question was --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It seems it is time for -- okay. I'll put this question after the break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes. But then perhaps -- the witness may be escorted out. There is some procedural matter that we will pursue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So we decided that we don't need to come back to the previous issue, and we take the adjournment now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We have been told that there is an issue that we should take care of before the witness comes in.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. It is in relation to the next witness. We're looking at the time that is left. I think that counsel for the Defence has about 22 minutes left. I expect to have perhaps about 20 minutes of re-examination. So that would take us a little bit past 1.30 roughly. Considering that the next witness is a protected witness and that he must not see the current witness, we were wondering if it would be more practical to begin the next witness tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes. Considering the time it would take to make sure that they don't cross in the -- in the building. Do you have a view on that, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wanted to ask the Trial Chamber to permit me, for example, 10 or 15 minutes more than I estimated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That now adds to the problem, and I think then, Mr. Demirdjian, that we will do as you propose, and we will schedule the next witness for tomorrow morning, 9.00. So the witness can be released for the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thanks. Can the witness be escorted in, Mr. Savic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Savic, I will repeat the question I put to you before the break. It concerns paragraph 70 of your statement where you say that following your release from prison and Zagreb, you broke off relations with Hadzic. You heard he called Ilija Koncarevic on the phone, and, among other things, you asked him why he was around people like Arkan. My question is: Did you ask him then or before that or when, really?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will answer, but could we briefly go to the previous document before that. I just wanted to check something. My name appears in the document as Borislav Savic, whereas my first name is Borivoje.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Does it mean that you did not testify on that day or that the record does not state your name correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did testify, but this record speaks of the accuracy of this document. I'd rather not go into detail about the nature of documents that appear there, but this very fact is an illustration of how trials are conducted before the War Crimes Chamber in Belgrade. If they can't get the name of the witness correctly, and to have that wrong name through the entire transcript speaks volumes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we look again at 1D6. It is first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your name as it appears here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see it on the first page. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page, then. The third page. On the fourth and fifth pages there are no names. Can we go to page 6. Page 7. Thus far, is your name correctly entered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but we'll get near the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Page 8. Page 9. Page 10. Eleven. Twelve. Thirteen. Fourteen. Fifteen. Sixteen. "Borislav" appears on page 16.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and on all following pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There seems to be a mistake, indeed. In any case, do you assert that what you said then is incorrect since we see the name "Borislav"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, it's got nothing to do with that. I told you I was there, although I had not had occasion to read the transcript, but it's just a feeling of how the trial developed and how it was conducted. As for the transcript itself, I see it for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is not customary to forward transcripts to witnesses, which is standard practice before our courts, and I believe elsewhere as well. In any case, there is an audio recording, and should there be any doubt as to the contents, we can always go back to that. Let us now go back to the question I put to you initially. In paragraph 70, you said that you were no longer in any kind of relationship with Goran Hadzic as of the day of your release from detention in Zagreb or the prison hospital because he called Ilija Koncarevic. You also said that you asked him why he was around people like Arkan. I'd like to know the following: Did you ask him that question then, the day you were returning to Slavonia and Vukovar, or at some other time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will answer. In the prison hospital, when we had arranged with the minister and his deputy to pick us up to take us home, we put our clothes on and went to the prison warden's office. I asked him if I could use his phone to call home.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this. Since I'm limited in terms of time, could you please focus on my question. I didn't ask you about you phoning. I wanted to know when you asked Goran Hadzic why he was around people like Arkan.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that moment, he called Koncarevic right after me. From time to time, depending on who he saw, the best of intentions, because I was neither his tutor nor mentor, but I asked him about Milosevic. I asked him about Arkan. Why do you walk around with Arkan? What right do you have? And he said, He's a good Serb. He's fighting for the Serb thing. So these were his general answers. I did not offer any comment on my part. It was up to him. Let me remind you of one thing. The area of his activity as the Vukovar board president was limited. Once he was out of the area of his activity, whatever he did was of his own accord and in his own name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's stop here, Mr. Savic. So you provided us with an answer. It was on that day when you asked him why he was around people like Arkan. My next question is: How do you know he socialised with Arkan? Where did you get that information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was on TV, in the media. Arkan boasted it about it himself, saying that the president assigned Erdut to him. The president of what assigned Erdut to him? Erdut was in Croatia, whereas his activities were in Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So it was based on TV information that you reached that conclusion, then. That is why you put that question to him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. All those people got in touch with me first, but I refused them. I did not want to go hand-in-hand with their activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You told us -- you said that on the 15th of May, when Vukasin Soskocanin drowned, you were in the Serbian Assembly building.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You also said in paragraph 159 of your statement, and you repeat that in the Stanisic and Simatovic case - if needed I can provide you with an exact reference - you said that you talked to Radmilo Bogdanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, what was Radmilo Bogdanovic's position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he was the security board president in the Assembly, or security committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you heard from him that a decision had been made that, as you put it in your statement, Arkan would be assigned to you, and you objected to it emphatically. Can you convey that dialogue between you and Bogdanovic briefly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can. I went to the Assembly building because I was invited by Pavic and Obradovic. The Assembly had a session that day. They usually sat until 5.00 p.m. The day before that, we were together on the riverbank across from Borovo Selo. I told him what had happened with Vukasin, and he told him -- he told me to come to the Assembly building once the session was over. I did so, and at 5.00, in Pavic's office, there was also Radmilo Bogdanovic. We greeted each other, and I was quite upset and tired after the whole day, and we moved from the office to a meeting room where there were other SPS members. I spoke to Radmilo briefly. I put forth my proposal on how to resolve the situation, and they agreed to it. After that, since I spoke quite openly and brusquely, he said, Calm down. And he said, You will now have Arkan as commander, and you will have Martic as the interior minister. So it wasn't that someone decided something. It was not an Assembly decision. The whole thing had to do with the premises where we discussed it. Radmilo was supposed to know how things were to develop, and he conveyed that information to me, and then I asked him to explain what it meant to send thieves and criminals to us. And he asked me, Do you think I will be held accountable for what I'm doing someday? I told him I was fully prepared to be called to task five years down the road to be held accountable for what I did. And he said, Well, I'll send him nevertheless. The next day, Janjackovic came, who I believe was a secretary in the Foreign Ministry, and when the meeting was over with the SUP chiefs from a number of towns along the Danube, he told me that Radmilo had said that we needed to talk so that you have an opportunity to say what you want. I responded that he should thank Radmilo for keeping his promise, but that in terms of such activities, I was -- I no longer wanted to be involved with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Soon after, you met Arkan, did you not? In the Stanisic and Simatovic case, you said it happened the next day, after you had conversed with Radmilo Bogdanovic in the Assembly. So that was on the 15th of May. Then what I'm talking about occurred on the 16th; right? The transcript reference is -- actually, it's OTP exhibit 4558. The page is 1810.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The meeting materialised. I was with Brane at the Matica building, and then a man came to pick me up, and right across the way from that building is a cafe, a pub called the Trident. Apparently it was owned by Arkan and a relative of his was in charge of running the place, but nobody went inside to sit down. Most of the guests were sitting outside because there was a garden out there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about the details of that conversation, because you described that in great detail.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and I stand by my previous account.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll just read for your benefit 1810, line 10: "[In English] Q. How many days after your conversation on the 15th of May with Mr. Bogdanovic did this meeting with Arkan occur? "A. On the following day." [Interpretation] That's all I want to know. Is that what you said at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that again the next day on cross-examination, but there's no need for me to go into that. As far as I've been able to tell based on your conversation with Arkan, you were quite brusque there. You told him a number of things that people would have found quite difficult to cope with in terms of being told straight to their face. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I agree fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So that occurred right after your conversation with Bogdanovic; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because I was taken aback by the fact that it happened so quickly and that he got it. But I never said anything specific against him. I stated what the situation was and that was that. It's not like he complained about it. It was a bit rough maybe, but there was nothing hostile about the tone of that conversation. You know, that's what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You see, Mr. Savic, we have information suggesting that at the time you claim you spoke to Radmilo Bogdanovic and when he told you that Arkan would become commander, and at the time when you allegedly met Arkan at the Trident, at the time Arkan was not in Belgrade. He was away. He wasn't even there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stand by my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll be showing you a document, 1D10. You see, this is a judgement of the Zagreb District Court on the 14th of June, 1991. Page 2 of the Serbian version shows you that this was a judgement passed. You see, if you look at page 1, page 1 has three names on it. And then the next page has the fourth name, the fourth accused. Zeljko Raznjatovic, aka Arkan. The remaining pages give us an account of what they stand accused of. At this point in time, we're not really interested in the substance of these charges, but we might go to what I think is page 10. The Serbian reference is -- it's the second-to-last page, I think. Page 5 in the Serbian. Page 4 in the English. If you look at this -- let me just check if we've got the right page of the English. It's the next page, please, in e-court. That's it. Thank you. So what we can see here is that on the 14th of June, 1991, the court sentenced Zeljko Raznjatovic and others to a prison sentence of one year and eight months. Time spent in detention will be taken into account, starting on the 29th of November to the 14th of June, 1991. This will become even more obvious based on 1D9. A letter written by the presiding judge of that particular Chamber of the Zagreb District Court. The letter was sent to the Zagreb District Prison, informing the prison that at the main hearing on the 14th of June, 1991, a ruling was made to terminate custody in relation to the accused named there, name number four on that list being Zeljko Raznjatovic. "A copy of the decision shall be submitted to you shortly," it reads. Finally, it says: "This order is to be executed immediately once it is received." Meaning, on the 14th of June, these men must be released.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would ask to tender these two documents, 1D10 and 1D9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 1D10 shall be assigned Exhibit Number D7. And 65 ter document 1D9 shall be assigned Exhibit Number D8. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You see, Mr. Savic, I'm looking at these two documents that I've just shown you, and they lead me to conclude that you were not telling the truth about your meeting and communication with Radmilo Bogdanovic on the 15th of May, 1990 [as interpreted], if indeed such a meeting ever materialised. And particularly, you weren't telling the truth about your communication with Zeljko Raznjatovic, nicknamed Arkan, which you claimed occurred at the time that he was in detention.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and then a government plane was dispatched to Zagreb to get those men. What I said about the Assembly, I stand by that. The conversation must then be moved in terms of the time line. Oversights are possible, of course. It's a fact, nevertheless, that I was told he would be the commander, and that's why he was dispatched to Zagreb, to become a hero, and that's why he was released. But that's a matter for another time. I did have this conversation with him, and I know that we were commenting on his time in prison in Croatia. We had both spent time in prison, so, you know, we talked about it. I was really surprised by how soon he got to know about this. So that's what the sense of priority was about, and that's why I said it is quite obvious that there was some communication going on behind them. The short time that it took, it couldn't be the next day, if indeed this is the case, but the conversation did take place. The communication did take place. So we can change the date, but what reason would I have to come up with a totally fictitious story about something that never happened? I think it's possible to go back to the municipal records, the Assembly records, showing what happened and when exactly, and there must be some information there about the date. At any rate, I also have witnesses, people who were with me. The person who drove me there to that meeting and another friend of mine from Odzaci, those men were with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, at 64, 15, the transcript says that the meeting with -- is on the 15th of May, 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I'll ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The meeting that you were talking about, it appears to have been misrecorded. It was on the 15th of May, 1990, the transcript says. But are we talking about 1990 or about 1991, the meeting at the Serbian Assembly, the day Soskocanin came to grief?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 1991. We're talking about 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Savic, you gave your first statement, and you said this in very categorical terms. That was back in 2002. You reiterated this in your evidence in the Stanisic and Simatovic trial under oath twice, as a matter of fact. You gave the same statement to the OTP, which is the one that has now been tendered and admitted, claiming that it is a truthful statement. And then again you took an oath when you came here, and you are now telling us that we can shift the dates a little bit. Nonetheless, that would be very difficult to exercise, if not actually impossible, wouldn't it, based on this? I'm not trying to challenge the possibility that you were at the Serbian Assembly, but I do challenge the theory that you discussed Arkan there, and I particularly challenge the theory that you met up with Arkan and spoke to him the way you have just described.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Assembly is true. The conversation is true. I may have been wrong about the date the conversation took place, but the conversation itself did materialise. That is true. This is nothing that is fabricated. There is no ill intention behind it, and I certainly added nothing to the substance of what actually transpired.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But you associate this conversation with a very peculiar event, the drowning, or as you suggest, the killing of Soskocanin, which you suggest -- or who you suggest was a close friend of yours. So establishing a link between these two facts, I can see that you needed a date, a specific date to get your bearings on that. On the other hand, you tell us you were surprised by how soon Arkan had found out about the substance of your conversation with Radmilo Bogdanovic. So a month after you talked to Radmilo Bogdanovic, Arkan was in fact in gaol. So how soon could this have possibly been, unless obviously Radmilo Bogdanovic talked to him the very first day he got out of gaol to tell him what he had been speaking to you about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Arkan was flown on a government plane from Zagreb. I expect that he was welcomed in an appropriate way once he got there. So let us not speculate. I talked to him in the way I described. The date was obviously a different one from the one that I had asserted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Savic. I have no more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Savic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Let me start with a few questions that were put to you by my learned friend yesterday, and for everyone in the courtroom, this was at page 620. It was put to you that there are 74 references to Slobodan Milosevic in your statement and that you had never met with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could we pull up the witness's statement which is admitted as P50, and in both versions could we go to page 5, please. Thank you. If we could scroll down to the bottom of paragraph 13. Yes. And the same in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: At the end of paragraph 13, Mr. Savic, do you see where you say -- well, you describe this exchange that Professor Raskovic had with Slobodan Milosevic. Do you see that part of the -- it's at the end of the paragraph. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And what was your source for this information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After appearing in Zagreb and in Croatia, professor would often go back to Belgrade, and that would often mean meeting Milosevic, who was then president. And then we'd always talk whenever he was back, what direction their reasoning and their thoughts were taking. So it was directly through talking to Professor Raskovic. And then we'd talk and I'd tell him to ask this question or that question when he was there but there was no need for me to go telling him, because his information was much more reliable and more extensive than mine. But your question about the source, the answer is directly from talking to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can we go to page 11 in both versions, please, and I would like to direct your attention to paragraph 35. And here you discuss the issue of the offer that was made by Tudjman to Professor Raskovic, and again here you explain what Raskovic told you about a conversation he had with Slobodan Milosevic. And again I'd like to ask you, very simply, what was the source of your information there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I told you about the situation and the position of the Serbs before and after the election. Professor Raskovic appeared as someone who was able to allay the tensions and give people hope. He was very much in the public eye at the time. He would appear on TV quite often. His visit to President Tudjman was shown on TV, and he congratulated Tudjman on his electoral victory. President Tudjman then told him, By tradition, you, the Serbs, should have the vice-president of the parliament. That was published in the press and in the public media at the time, and it was confirmed to me by Professor Raskovic himself. Nevertheless, when I asked him, Why did you not accept, and he said Milosevic did not agree. And then instead of Professor Raskovic, they decided to appoint Jovo Opacic but then Tudjman turned him down. The parliament was constituted and everything just went on in a totally different direction and they didn't talk about this anymore. Nevertheless, there was a real offer on the table, and even the media recorded the fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I'm not going to go through each of the 74 examples. Let's take one last example at page 22, please, in both versions. And I would like to direct your attention to paragraph 79. And here you describe the position that was held by Hadzic vis-a-vis Mr. Milosevic. Now, this information you provide in your statement here about Milosevic, who gave you that information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard that from Ilija Koncarevic. Before the Serbian National Council was established, he came to see me at my home and he said, Tomorrow we'll be going -- the next day we'll be going to Belgrade to see the president. Which route shall we take? We'll pick up Jugoslav Kostic on the way there and then we'll go to Belgrade to set up the National Council. So it was a real offer that was made. I said I'd have no part in that, that I wouldn't be involved, and that I wouldn't be going. That was the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Savic, I was pointing to paragraph 79, and specifically the question -- the sentence where it says: "Goran would also tell me how good Milosevic was and that Milosevic was not interested in power," et cetera, et cetera. Where did you get that information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I asked him during one of the rides when we were together. One had to travel ten hours to get to Knin. It all added up. I asked him, Please explain your relationship with Milosevic to me. He said, He's a good man, and it was something along the lines as noted in the statement. However, my question was not in terms of making a suggestion. I had the best intention in mind, and he just provided information. In any case, he's aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. I'll move away from this topic. Yesterday, at page 631 and 632, my learned friend put to you questions about the concept of Ustasha. And when you were asked about it, I believe that you were interrupted and you were in the midst of saying that this is a concept that was abused, and could you please expand on that now, because the question to you was about the use of the word "Ustasha" in World War II, and please, could you expand on that now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The concept of the Ustasha movement needs not be explained any further as a movement, but you're interested in the term, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I'm interested at the moment where you were interrupted. You were talking about the fact that the concept was being abused, and this was when you were talking about the conflict in 1990, 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes. It was used to irritate, to create negative energy, negative feelings. On one side it could have a positive effect, while on the other it had a negative effect. It a means to manipulate people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And could you tell us what was the consequence of the use of the term "Ustasha"? What impact did it have at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Among Serbs, it reminded them of the crimes of the Ustasha in Second World War, and one you had -- one had this constant reiteration of the locations of people being killed and all the crimes committed during the time of the Independent State of Croatia back then. It was justified in a way because it evoked certain memories. There were people who had lost their entire families and only individuals survived by chance. Such Ustasha crimes happened during the Second World War. When I used the term that it was abused, I had in mind that there was no necessity to increase fear and anxiety even further in such turbulent times. That's why I said that it was abused.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Moving on to another topic, you told the Court at page 649 that at one point government members told you that you were banned from communicating with them, and you heard this from Bogdan Vorkapic, and you also mentioned the name of Milos Vojnovic. Did any of them tell you who did not allow you -- or did not allow them to speak to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The sequence of events was quite logical. The first offers to create the National Council and get engaged in such activities was made to me during the initial months, but I refused. I also didn't want to burden anyone or raise tensions by opening up unnecessary topics. And then things took a different direction, and other people became involved, and all the events surrounding the establishment of government and the National Council was the result of fabrications. There was never an act of establishment or anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Savic, I think we would all be assisted, and you as well, if you would listen carefully to the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The question is who told you? Did anyone of those people who were banned to communicate with you, did anyone of these people tell you so? So that's the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The people are mentioned, Bogdan Vorkapic. So there are people by name who said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: In this specific --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Sorry. Now, I wandered a little bit off. It's not who told you, but the question was: Did they tell you who ordered them not to communicate with you? That was your question, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: That was the question. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who established it. I didn't ask. I didn't insist to know. Well, banned, so what? But who established the government? That's what you can't see anywhere. That's what it's about. I don't think it was done by our people who were made part of the government. Those who established it should say. Someone had to establish it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: They didn't tell you the name of the person or the institution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You were asked several questions about your concerns about being liquidated at the time, and you repeated on a few occasions that you don't suffer from paranoia. Let me ask you, Mr. Savic, when was Vukasin Soskocanin killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 15th of May, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And you mentioned in your statement at paragraphs 137 to 139 the killing of Josip Reihl-Kir and you explained that he was the chief of police in Osijek. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Josip Reihl-Kir. He was the chief of police in Osijek. He was an exceptionally brave man, full of energy, and he worked in an exceedingly dangerous environment when people like Seks and Glavas were in power. Seks even publicly called on the population not to turn to the police any longer but to the HDZ. He participated in all peace meetings and attempts in the area. He even came to Borovo Selo, which was part of the Vukovar municipality. It was a neighbouring municipality. Dalj and Bijelo Brdo were in the Osijek municipality, whereas he came to Borovo Selo as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And his killing, I believe you mentioned in your statement was -- let me see if you mentioned a date here. Can we go to the next page, paragraph 139. I don't believe it said. Do you recall when he was killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't recall the date, but I founded the association of victims of the Croatian regime in 1991 in Krajina. All those who were victims became members, and one of the members was Mirko Tubic, who was the president of the local commune in Tenja who survived it. He put forth all the details surrounding that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. I believe we have documents which will support this at a later stage, but would it be roughly correct to say that he was killed around June or July of 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: June or July, yes. I don't know a precise date, but around that time. I even think it was in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And was this the same time period that you had concerned for -- that you had concerns about your own safety?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, fighting political opponents in our part of the world may well mean having them liquidated. It's not a secret. In any case, someone who doesn't go hand-in-hand with the ideas of those in power is in the sphere of danger, and one better watch his back at such times.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Let me finish off with the questions that were put to you about Lovas. You were shown --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: First of all, can we pull up Exhibit P79.50.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: These are -- this is the agenda or the minutes that you typed up. And you were asked about the positions of the various individuals listed here. Now, just to be clear, this is the retyped format of notes you had taken; is that right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: When did you take the notes, the original ones?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Sorry. When did you take the original notes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You were asked about Stevo Bogic, and it says here "Deputy Prime Minister and State Security Chief." Can you tell the Court based on what information you wrote that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I took the notes on the spot. The chief of the state service was there, but there was also a lower-level official, I believe. But they all said he was the vice-president of something or other. I'd be hard put to say. Municipal vice-president, or candidate for municipal vice-president in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, another set of notes were shown to you. This is Exhibit D6. We can pull that up too. And before we look at the document -- well, let's pull it up in the meantime. Mr. Savic, did you ever present yourself as Borivoje Savic from Lovas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I never presented myself like that, but I was, as a matter of fact, in Lovas at the time, so I may have recorded "Lovas." But Lovas was not a part of my personal information.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. Can we go to the page before last in both versions. In English it's one page before that. Yes. Can we scroll down a bit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, under number 12 you see "Borislav Bogunovic"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, which town is written next to his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, this is the 30th of October, 1991. Do you happen to know where Mr. Bogunovic was in October 1991? Was he in Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. He was in Sid.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. I cannot see your name on this. It's probably on the next page in the English version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's on the next page, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: So in the English it's one more page. Yes. The next page in English. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you told the Court that this was not your handwriting; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not the word "Lovas," and not the part where it says "TO member." Those two bits were added. If you can actually zoom in, you can compare the letters that I wrote.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. We can put this document away now. And in relation to Lovas, Mr. Savic, you were asked about -- you were shown excerpts from your testimony, and you were asked when you heard from General Nenezic that the army, and these are the words used in the document, that the army had screwed up in Lovas? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's difficult to say the date when all these people were coming and going and all of this was going on. The report from the field would be submitted to the KOS in Belgrade, and all those who were in charge of that were in a position to find out. I'm not sure which term to use, but it was after this happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And at the time, you're telling us that General Nenezic was a retired general from the KOS; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Just for the sake of completeness, can we pull up 65 ter 1D00006. In the B/C/S version we can go to page 18, and in the English version we can go to page 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, this excerpt was shown to you by my learned friend, and at least in the English version, somewhere in the middle of the page you were asked when did you hear that the army had screwed up? And is that your answer there: "Sometime before my arrival in Lovas"? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, General Nenezic was a retired general. How would he have access to this information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The KOS never dies. When people retire, they still have their communication channels. They still have sources. It's just for curiosity's sake. People still continue to talk to each other on a daily basis. You know, they just talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Savic. These are all the questions that I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Savic, this brings your testimony to an end. We thank you for coming to The Hague to assist the Tribunal, and we wish you a safe journey home. The usher will now escort you out of court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I could just raise a small procedural matter for tomorrow's witness it might make things go more smoothly tomorrow. There are currently three exhibits that the Prosecution would like to use with the next witness. They are 65 ter 6331, 6334, and 6338.1, and those are all exhibits that were included in the most recent Prosecution motion to add things to its 65 ter list, the fourth 65 ter motion, and in the motion the Prosecution had indicated that it wished to use those exhibits with -- with tomorrow's witness. There's a fourth exhibit which is 65 ter 6237, which the Chamber does not have. We've been in communication with the Defence about it. It is one of the Google Map satellite images that actually has been accepted, but what we found was we wanted to sort of zoom out just a little bit to include a wider area on that image, and it was -- we've asked the Defence, actually, a couple times whether they would agree to our substituting this -- this one for the previous one that is a bit more narrow, and so we're not asking for any rulings. It would be nice to know what the Defence position is in respect of these four exhibits before we start with the witness tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, could I ask you about the last one. That seems to be an easy answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, there are no objections to any of the four documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: No objections to any of them. Thank you very much. So we reconvene tomorrow at 9.00 in this courtroom. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 1st day of November, 2012, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
